headline: Salt crystals could hold clues to life beneath Enceladus's ice
author: Andrew Zinin

paragraphs.text: October 17, 2026 report
by Andrew Zinin, Phys.org
edited by Lisa Lock, reviewed by Robert Egan

The ocean beneath Saturn's moon Enceladus lies under kilometers of ice, but some of its contents do reach the surface. Jets near the south pole spray out water vapor and icy particles, offering a way to investigate the hidden ocean without drilling down to it.

The challenge is knowing which material preserves the most useful clues. A new laboratory study points to a possible target: salt crystals that trap tiny pockets of water as they grow during freezing.

Liam Perera of Diamond Light Source in the United Kingdom and colleagues found these pockets inside natron, a sodium carbonate mineral expected to form on Enceladus. Their findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, suggest that the crystals could preserve information about the ocean's chemistry—and potentially traces of life, if any exists there.
Trapping water inside salt

To determine which surface mineral would be the best candidate, the team cooled a solution containing sodium chloride and sodium carbonate, using powerful X-rays to watch it freeze. Three-dimensional images revealed the growing crystals and their interiors, and measurements of how the crystals scattered X-rays identified the minerals present.

As natron grew, it enclosed pockets of the surrounding fluid. Larger crystals were more likely to contain these pockets and tended to hold larger samples. Only about 3% of nearly 3,800 separated grains contained fluid inclusions, as researchers call them, but all 29 grains in the largest size category did.
That makes the crystals potentially useful containers: Each pocket could retain a small sample of the water present when it closed.

There is an earthly reason to consider what else might be trapped. Earlier research on ancient salt deposits reported possible microbial cells preserved in fluid pockets inside crystals formed as water evaporated.

Although the new experiment shows that natron can trap fluid during freezing, whether it can also capture and preserve biological material remains untested. The authors propose that the surrounding mineral could help shield any such material from damaging radiation.
What type of water would a crystal capture?
A trapped sample would not necessarily be an unchanged drop of Enceladus's ocean, however.

The researchers used a solution about five times more concentrated than the estimates based on particles sampled by NASA's Cassini spacecraft. This helped produce crystals large enough to examine. In that concentrated mixture, large natron crystals began growing before the main ice formation, enclosing fluid that was expected to remain close to the starting composition.

In a more dilute, ocean-like solution, ice would probably form first. As it grew, it would leave dissolved salts behind, concentrating the remaining water. Natron forming later would capture that saltier liquid.

Yet both could tell researchers something useful: One would provide a closer record of the original water, while the other would reveal how freezing changed it. The crystals' shapes and the material around them could help distinguish those histories. At Enceladus's surface temperatures, the trapped water itself would be frozen.
Where to look

Natron, although a leading candidate for astrobiological study, has yet to be confirmed on Enceladus's surface. The team recommends that future spacecraft carry sensitive near-infrared instruments to identify it and guide sampling.

Fresh deposits near the plume vents could be particularly promising sources. Larger droplets should cool more slowly, giving crystals time and space to grow; very rapid cooling could prevent natron from crystallizing. The researchers propose that larger, salt-rich particles are also more likely to fall back near the vents.
Finding the mineral would therefore be only part of the search. Its location and condition would matter, too.

Natron should remain stable in the moon's extreme cold, but warmer terrain near the vents could gradually strip water from its crystal structure. Recently deposited crystals could offer the best combination: material delivered from the interior, with its microscopic pockets still intact.
